name: Cruise berth, Tourist Port (Akti Sachtouri)
sub: Where the day starts. Berth varies: if the ship is sent to Akandia, add ten minutes.
blurb: Scarlet Lady's likely berth on the quay east of the walls. The published schedules put her here 09:00 to 18:00 alongside Celestyal Discovery (07:00 to 18:00); the port fund's own list of late August also names Costa Fortuna and Gemini that morning, so expect three or four ships and a busy Palace from mid-morning. Face the walls: this whole waterfront is the ancient Great Harbour that Demetrius attacked with ship-mounted siege towers in 305 BC. If the ship is berthed at Akandia instead, walk north along the water; the Gate of the Virgin is about ten minutes.
dnd: The party disembarks in a harbour once closed by a floating boom of spiked logs and fire-ships packed with pitch.

name: Gate of the Virgin (Pyli Panagias)
sub: The threshold. Look back at the ship, then walk through.
blurb: The nearest opening in the sea wall to the cruise quay, cut in 1955 on an Italian plan. Stop before the arch and turn around: ship, harbour, medieval stone all in one frame. Then walk through. The Italian tongue's stretch of wall ran south from here to the harbour corner.

name: Our Lady of the Burgh (Panagia tou Bourgou)
sub: A Gothic church with no roof. Three apses still stand against the sky.
blurb: The roofless 14th-century Gothic church of Our Lady of the Burgh, three apses open to the sky, just inside the gate that carries its name. Christian, then Ottoman, then bombed, now a garden of arches. The audio trick: ten seconds of choir and stone reverb, then cut to the real wind.
dnd: A ruined chapel at the edge of the outer ward: the classic place to find the first clue.

name: Hippocrates Square and the Castellania
sub: Hub of the lower town. The Knights' courthouse of 1507, an owl on the fountain, a wine cellar under the stairs.
blurb: The heart of the Burgh, the merchants' town the Knights ruled but did not live in. The Castellania (1507) with its outside staircase was the Order's court; a stone owl tops the fountain. Ignore the table-hustlers here; the good restaurants are one lane off. Under the Castellania stairs, the Cellar of Knights has poured Rhodian wine by the glass since 1963.
dnd: The town square where the quest-giver posts the notice. The tavern under the courthouse stairs is where rumours are bought.
hours: Public square; Cellar of Knights Wed 11:00 to 23:00

name: Marine Gate (Thalassini Pyli)
sub: D'Aubusson's harbour gate of 1478. Tell the Rhodian Sea Law here.
blurb: Twin round towers built by Grand Master d'Aubusson in 1478, wrecked by Allied bombs and restored in 1951; look for the saints in relief above the arch. From this quay the Knights sailed away on 1 January 1523. This is the place for the Rhodian Sea Law, the ancient rule on jettison that still lives in every marine insurance policy, and the emperor Antoninus' reply to a shipwrecked merchant: I am Lord of the World, but the Law is Lord of the sea.
dnd: The exodus gate: fifty ships, drums beating, a new banner of the Pieta. A merchant-navy guild whose code even emperors bow to.

name: Hospital of the Knights (Archaeological Museum)
sub: The Order's reason for existing. The marble head of Helios, the Aphrodite of Rhodes, the Marine Venus.
blurb: Begun 1440, finished 1489 under d'Aubusson: a monumental stair, a great ward with seven octagonal pillars where knights nursed the sick in person. Inside, the over-life-size head of Helios with drilled sockets for a bronze ray-crown, the closest surviving face to the Colossus; the crouching Aphrodite of Rhodes; the sea-worn Marine Venus that Durrell watched rise from her wartime crypt; the stele of Krito and Timarista. Go early, before two ships' worth of visitors arrive.
dnd: A lawful-good order's healing hall, now a reliquary holding a sun-god's severed marble head.
hours: Wed 30 Sep: 08:00 to 20:00 (official summer schedule to 31 Oct). The Prehistoric exhibition is open Wed 09:00 to 17:00; the Epigraphical exhibition and Villaragut Mansion are closed on Wednesdays.

name: Street of the Knights (Odos Ippoton)
sub: Two hundred metres uphill through the inns of the tongues. Read the shields as you climb.
blurb: Right-hand side going up: Inn of Italy (1519, Grand Master Carretto's shield), Inn of France (the richest facade: corner turret, crocodile gargoyles for the dragon legend, d'Aubusson's cardinal's hat, three plaques of l'Isle-Adam), the tiny Holy Trinity chapel (1365 to 1374, papal arms framed by the lions of England), the chaplain's house with ten shields on its lintel. Left: the Inn of Spain, and the Inn of Provence joined to it by the arch overhead. The Italians stripped the Ottoman balconies in 1916; the stone and heraldry are original.
dnd: Guild street of a warrior order. Each inn is a faction chapter-house: France gave the Hospitaller, Italy the Admiral, Auvergne the Marshal, England the Turcopolier, Aragon the standard-bearer, Castile the Chancellor, Germany the Grand Bailiff, Provence the Grand Commander. Four of the last five Grand Masters were Frenchmen, two of them from the Inn of France.

name: Site of St John of the Collachium (the vault that exploded)
sub: The Order's church, six Grand Masters' tombs, the Baptist's right hand. Blown up in 1856.
blurb: Where the neoclassical school and the clock tower now stand was the Knights' conventual church, begun about 1310: tombs of at least six Grand Masters including the dragon-slayer Gozon, and the treasury of relics, among them the right hand of John the Baptist (one tradition has it here from 1413, another says Sultan Bayezid II sent it in 1484 to sweeten the deal that kept his rival brother a prisoner of the Knights). After 1522 it became the main mosque. On 6 November 1856 lightning struck the gunpowder stored in the cellars under its bell tower; the blast levelled the church, gutted the Palace and killed at least 200 people. Only scraps of foundation show beside the school; Gozon's plain tomb slab went to Paris in 1877, and the Italians rebuilt the church from engravings at Mandraki.
dnd: A reliquary chapel over a forgotten powder magazine: a dungeon trap with a 334-year fuse. The dragon-slayer's tomb is now in the Musee de Cluny.

name: Palace of the Grand Master
sub: The keep on the sun's hill. Probably where the Colossus actually stood.
blurb: A Byzantine citadel on the small hill at the head of the Collachium, the Order's headquarters from 1309, wrecked in 1856 and rebuilt 1937 to 1940 for Victor Emmanuel III and Mussolini, who never came. Upstairs, mosaics lifted from Kos (the Medusa, the Nine Muses) and a cast of the Laocoon, carved by Rhodians. Downstairs on a Wednesday: the Ancient Rhodes exhibition, with the stone shot from Demetrius' siege engines, the very sale that paid for the Colossus. Nathan Badoud's 2024 Oxford study puts the sanctuary of Helios, and the statue, on this hill. Buy the walls-walk ticket at the desk.
dnd: A crusader citadel on a buried sun-temple, later a dictator's summer palace paved with looted mosaics. Grain silos under the courtyard for sieges.
hours: Wed 30 Sep: 08:00 to 20:00, last admission 20 minutes before closing (official page). Inside, exactly one of the two big exhibitions is open on a Wednesday, 09:00 to 17:00, and the Ministry's two pages disagree on which (the newer one says Ancient Rhodes); the Knights-to-Malta room and the gardens are daily 09:00 to 17:00. Phone +30 22413 65270 to check. Leaving and re-entering for the walls walk means paying again, so go in about 11:00.
price: EUR 20, which the Ministry page says is also valid for the Archaeological Museum, Decorative Arts and Our Lady of the Castle; walls walk EUR 5 to 6 extra

name: D'Amboise Gate (the dragon's head)
sub: Triple gate of 1512. The 'dragon' skull hung over a gate here until about 1837.
blurb: Emery d'Amboise's gate of 1512, the grandest in the circuit: a marble angel with the arms of the Order, drawbridge slots in the twin round towers, three dog-legged gates behind (the Ottomans called it the Crooked Gate). Local tradition says the head of the dragon slain by Dieudonne de Gozon hung over this gate until workmen threw it out around 1837 to 1839. Everyone who saw it described a crocodile. Stand under the arch and look up.
dnd: Trophy over the gate. On a Nature check it is a Nile crocodile. Quest hook: whose crocodile was it?

name: Walls walk: iron gate on the Palace forecourt
sub: Weekdays 12:00 to 15:00 only. Walk the faction map on top of the ramparts.
blurb: Buy the ticket at the Palace desk, then find the unsigned iron gate on the forecourt by the Gate of St Anthony, with a custodian checking tickets. One-way along the top of the west and south curtain, about 1.6 km, no railings on the inside, no shade, 45 to 90 minutes. Each stretch belonged to one tongue and carries its arms: France, Germany, Auvergne, Spain (the tower taken and retaken on 24 September 1522), England (mined on 4 September 1522), Provence, Italy.
dnd: The wall is a faction map you walk across, over the moat where forty Ottoman mines met Tadini's counter-mines.
hours: Mon to Fri 12:00 to 15:00, closed weekends (consistent 2025 and 2026 visitor reports; not on the official page). Confirm at the ticket desk.

name: Gate of St John (Koskinou, the Red Gate): walls walk end
sub: Where the rampart walk comes down. Named for the blood of 1522, by legend.
blurb: The south-east corner where the walls walk drops down steep concrete steps. Kokkini Porta, the Red Gate, because the legend says the blood of the 1522 dead dyed its stones. Suleiman made his second ceremonial entry through this gate on 29 December 1522 and went down to admire the harbour chain. The Jewish quarter is five minutes north.
hours: Gate always open; walls exit only during the walk

name: Kahal Shalom Synagogue and Jewish Museum
sub: Oldest synagogue in Greece (1577). Open Wed 10:00 to 15:00.
blurb: Sephardic plan with the bimah in the centre and, unusually, two Torah arks; the only one of the quarter's synagogues to survive the 1944 bombing. The museum next door fills the old women's prayer rooms with the photographs and archives of a Ladino-speaking community of 4,000. On 23 July 1944, 1,673 people were marched from here to the harbour; about 151 came back. The Turkish consul Selahattin Ulkumen saved some 42 to 50 by insisting that under Turkish law all citizens are equal.
dnd: The one sanctuary that survived the bombardment, keeping the memory-books of a vanished community. Leave silence at the end of this track.
hours: Sun to Fri 10:00 to 15:00, closed Saturdays and state holidays (1 Apr to 31 Oct). 30 Sep is an intermediate day of Sukkot; no closure is listed, but confirm by email jcrhodes@otenet.gr.

name: Square of the Jewish Martyrs
sub: Six-language memorial of 2002 and the bronze seahorse fountain.
blurb: The assembly point of July 1944. The black six-sided memorial (dedicated 23 June 2002) speaks in English, French, Greek, Hebrew, Italian and Judaeo-Spanish; the seahorse fountain a few steps east is the square's older, gentler landmark. In 1480 the fighting reached this quarter and Jewish houses were pulled down for rubble to reinforce the wall behind it. La Veranda's rooftop overlooks the square if you want the view with lunch.

name: Lunch: Nireas, Sofokleous 22
sub: Birthday lunch under a 25-year-old vine. Symi shrimp, grilled dorade, panna cotta with figs.
blurb: The Tsikis family's seafood taverna since 1989, under a pergola of jasmine and bougainvillea on a small square where the bazaar noise stops. Symi shrimp, scallops, calamari, grilled dorade, then panna cotta with figs. Sofokleous is the one quiet good street in the walled town: Romios (modern Rhodian, plated) is at number 15 and Pizanias at 24. Book: +30 22410 21703.
dnd: The tavern behind the bazaar where the noise stops; one family has kept it for a generation.

name: Roloi clock tower, Suleymaniye and the Ottoman library
sub: Fifty-three steps, four windows, one drink included. The Ottoman crown of the town.
blurb: The highest point inside the walls. The 1852 Ottoman clock tower on a Byzantine base, rebuilt after the 1856 blast: 53 steep wooden steps to a chamber with four small windows, Palace north, Monte Smith west, the harbour and your ship east, the minaret south-east. Five euros includes a beer, wine or coffee in the courtyard bar: the natural birthday toast. Below, the rose-pink Suleymaniye Mosque (first mosque of the conquest, rebuilt 1808, 34.5 m minaret re-erected 1988 to 2005) and, across the lane, the Hafiz Ahmed Agha Library of 1793, holding about 1,260 manuscripts including a chronicle of the 1522 siege.
dnd: The conqueror's temple raised on the defeated faction's shrine, with the town's arcane library across the lane, kept by a custodian who literally holds the door code.
hours: Roloi: hours not officially published; listed 09:00 to 21:00 in season. Mosque interior closed since 2014 and only irregularly open. Library hours are posted on its door only.

name: Temple of Aphrodite, Symi Square (the Telchines)
sub: A 3rd-century BC temple built a generation after the Colossus. Tell the sorcerer-smiths here.
blurb: A fenced tumble of column drums and a podium just inside Liberty Gate: the only Hellenistic temple you can touch in the walled town. This is the spot for the Telchines, the island's first inhabitants in myth: sorcerer-smiths who forged the sickle of Cronus, summoned rain and hail, changed shape, poisoned crops with Styx water and sulphur, and had the evil eye. Diodorus says the sons of the Telchine Halia drove Aphrodite from this shore and she cursed them with madness.
dnd: A vanished guild of artificer-warlocks, a goddess's curse, and a divine flood as the world's first cataclysm. Legendary artifact: the Sickle of Cronus.

name: Liberty Gate (1924)
sub: Out of the medieval city into the Italian one. The score opens into stereo here.
blurb: Cut through the walls by the Italians in 1924, who named it for themselves as liberators from Ottoman rule. Step through and the Foro Italico begins: the Nea Agora (closed for restoration in 2026), the Bank of Greece, the Governor's Palace done as a Doge's Palace, the Evangelismos church rebuilt from engravings of the Knights' church that exploded in 1856.
dnd: A gate that is not on the old dungeon map because the new rulers cut it themselves.

name: The deer columns, Mandraki harbour mouth
sub: Where every postcard puts the Colossus's feet. Read the dedication here.
blurb: Two limestone columns raised in 1939 under the Italian administration, topped by Renato Brozzi's bronze stag Elafos and doe Elafina, 62 m apart, marking the spot tradition gives the statue's feet. Read the pedestal epigram aloud here. Then look across the water to the windmill mole and the fort: in 1394 a visiting notary was told the statue had one foot on each. That is about 400 m. No bronze figure can stride it, and Pliny saw the wreck lying on ground you could walk around.
dnd: Twin guardian-beast pillars at a harbour gate; a Fascist-era monument that survived by being mistaken for ancient.

name: Fort St Nicholas, tip of the Mandraki mole
sub: The tower that broke the 1480 siege, and one candidate for the Colossus's pedestal. Best free 360-degree view.
blurb: Built 1464 to 1467 by Grand Master Zacosta over a chapel of St Nicholas, ringed with a bastion by d'Aubusson after 1480, a lighthouse on top since the 1600s. Mesih Pasha's first target in 1480: bombarded from the shore by the Murad Reis mosque, stormed on 9 June, and on the night of 18 June an English sailor swam out and cut the anchor of the Ottoman pontoon bridge. Wolfram Hoepfner (2003) argued the Colossus stood right here; a ring of sandstone blocks under the floor is the clue. Interior closed for restoration; walk the mole and turn around.
dnd: A lighthouse-keep on a causeway, a pontoon bridge creeping across black water, one swimmer with a knife. Under the floor, maybe, the footprint of a bronze god.
hours: Mole open always; interior treat as closed

name: Swan by Kontiki (floating bar, Mandraki)
sub: Three floating decks off the New Market quay. The unnecessarily nice birthday cocktail.
blurb: Successor to the old Kontiki floating cafe: three levels moored off Plateia Neoriou, coffee and brunch 10:00 to 13:00, then sushi, oysters and cocktails on the top deck with the windmills, the fort and the walls in one sweep. Expensive (mains EUR 37 to 52, oysters EUR 9 each) and 2026 reviews are split on service. One drink on the top deck, mid-afternoon light, then walk. Book: +30 697 254 3322.
dnd: The ship-tavern that never sails, anchored where legend puts the Colossus's feet.

name: Naillac tower stump and St Paul's Gate
sub: A 46-metre lighthouse-keep that held the harbour chain, split by the 1863 earthquake.
blurb: On the mole east of St Paul's Gate is the base of the square Tower of Naillac (1396 to 1421), 46 m high, lighthouse, watchtower and anchor of the great chain that closed the commercial harbour at night, stretched across to the Tower of the Windmills on the far mole; in 1522 the Order's fleet sheltered behind it and Suleiman came down to admire it. The earthquake of 22 April 1863 split the tower and the Ottoman administration pulled the rest down: the last of the fortifications to die, and not to an army. Pilgrims felt the harbour's wariness: Felix Fabri, arriving by moonlight weeks after the 1480 siege, was fired on by a cannon, made to anchor outside, and rowed in next morning through the bodies of dead Turks cast up by the sea. From here it is a level 12-minute walk along the quay to the ship.
dnd: A fallen watchtower and a broken chain, killed by the ground itself.

name: Temple of Apollo Pythios, Monte Smith (Vedder's site)
sub: Four re-erected Doric columns on the acropolis. Ursula Vedder says this was Helios's sanctuary.
blurb: The columns you can see from the harbour crown the acropolis hill 3 km south-west (taxi about 10 minutes, or a 35-minute uphill walk from the Gate of St Athanasios). Ursula Vedder (2015) re-identifies this temple as the sanctuary of Helios and reads the ruin north-east of it as the Colossus's base and workshop. Robert Kebric (2019) puts the statue higher still, on the summit by the Temple of Athena Polias, as a beacon for all five harbours. In 2025 visitors found the columns fenced and scaffolded; the view is the reason to come.
dnd: A temple mislabelled for a century, its true god hidden in plain sight; casting pits nearby where a bronze titan was forged in sections.

name: Summit of Monte Smith (Kebric's site) and the nymphaea
sub: The treaty-temple of the city, Posidonius' tower, and where a second colossus was offered to Rome in 167 BC.
blurb: The limestone shelf at the top of the acropolis held the Temple of Athena Polias and Zeus Polieus, where the city kept its treaties. Robert Kebric argues the Colossus stood here as a light-tower for the harbours. This is also the place for Posidonius, the Stoic under whom Rhodes eclipsed Athens: Pompey, conqueror of East and West, lowered his fasces at his door; he lectured from his sickbed that pain is no evil; Cicero saw his orrery, a bronze sphere that showed the sun, moon and five planets moving; he measured the Earth from the star Canopus grazing this horizon; and the Antikythera mechanism, which uses Hipparchus' lunar theory and was found on a wreck carrying Rhodian pottery, may have been built in his circle. Between the summit and the Apollo terrace are four rock-cut nymphaea, cave sanctuaries with cisterns and niches. The ridge is named for Admiral Sidney Smith, posted here in the early 1800s to watch for Napoleon's fleet.
dnd: The archmage's tower: a general kneels at the door, a clockwork cosmos ticks inside, and the artifact in the Athens museum may have been forged here. Cave-shrines beneath.

name: Windmills of Mandraki (the 'other mole')
sub: Three surviving mills of thirteen. In 1394 locals said the statue's second foot stood here.
blurb: Three restored medieval windmills line the mole that shelters the commercial harbour, survivors of thirteen built 1420 to 1483 to grind grain for the Knights. Niccolo de Martoni was told in 1394 that the Colossus rested one foot by the church of St Nicholas and the other 'on the end of the other mole where the mills are'. From here, look north to the fort and measure the impossible stride. Good birthday-portrait spot with the walls behind you.

name: Evangelismos church (the Italians' replica of St John's)
sub: Built 1924 to 1929 from engravings of the Knights' church that exploded in 1856. Kontoglou's frescoes inside.
blurb: Florestano Di Fausto's Gothic reconstruction of the Knights' conventual church of St John, begun 1924 and opened as the Italian cathedral, converted after 1948 into the Orthodox cathedral of the Annunciation; Fotis Kontoglou frescoed the interior in neo-Byzantine style through the 1950s. It stands 100 m from the deer columns, so the medieval church and its Italian resurrection sit side by side with the Colossus legend.
dnd: A temple raised from memory by a foreign order, then re-consecrated by another and painted with a new pantheon of saints.

name: Bastion of St George (tunnels rigged to collapse)
sub: Pentagonal prototype of the modern bastion, finished before 1522. The terreplein behind it was honeycombed with galleries.
blurb: Built after 1480 around a gate tower d'Aubusson had walled shut, and given its final pentagonal form by the Vicenza engineer Basilio della Scuola before 1522; the arms of the last Grand Master, Villiers de l'Isle-Adam, sit above. Historians call it a prototype of the angled bastion that defined European fortresses for 300 years. The terreplein of Spain behind it held underground passages designed to be collapsed on any attacker who got into them. Somewhere on this stretch, the post of Auvergne, the Chancellor's servant was caught with a bow and a letter in October 1522.
dnd: A sealed gate, a five-pointed fort, tunnels built to be blown under the enemy's feet. The traitor's crossbow bolt was fired from this rampart.

name: Tower of Spain (taken and retaken, 24 September 1522)
sub: Janissary banners on the rampart by noon; knights came back through the tunnels.
blurb: On 24 September 1522, the day of the great general assault, the Janissaries took this tower by midday and planted their standards on the rampart. Fra Jacques de Bourbon led the knights back through the underground passages and retook it; it changed hands twice before Suleiman called off the attack and sentenced his commander Mustafa Pasha to death, then relented. The Spanish position finally fell on 17 or 18 December, and the city capitulated within days.
dnd: The contested tower. Enemy standards on the battlements at noon; underground, sappers meeting in the dark.

name: Terreplein of England (the mines and the drum)
sub: Two mines blew a 12-yard breach here on 4 September 1522. Tadini listened for the sappers with a drum.
blurb: The English post between the gates of St Athanasios and St John. At dawn on 4 September 1522 two Ottoman mines opened a breach here; the English brothers under Fra Nicholas Hussey and the Grand Master in person held it all day. Against forty or more Ottoman tunnels the Venetian engineer Gabriele Tadini pressed a drum with bells on its skin against the gallery walls to hear the picks, then blew the enemy tunnel from below or broke in for close-quarters fighting. He took an arquebus ball through the eye on 14 October and was leading a sortie six weeks later.
dnd: Mines and counter-mines: a listening drum with silver bells, forty tunnels, powder charges set beneath the enemy's own charge. Roll for perception.

name: Del Carretto bastion (the 1480 breach)
sub: Where 2,500 Janissaries got over the wall on 27 July 1480, and a vision was reported above the breach.
blurb: The huge round cannon platform of Grand Master Fabrizio del Carretto sits exactly on the weak south-east angle held by the Italian tongue, backing on the Jewish quarter. Ottoman guns pounded it to rubble; at dawn on 27 July 1480 the Janissaries took the Tower of Italy and planted their standards. D'Aubusson climbed his brick retrenchment three times and took five wounds, one a lance into the lung; then the assault broke. The Order's vice-chancellor Caoursin wrote that the Turks saw a golden cross and a virgin in white with a spear above the wall. Propaganda, brilliantly done. The Akandia Gate beside it is the southern entrance to the moat.
dnd: The breach: enemy banners on the tower, a half-dead commander on a ladder, a divine apparition that may have been a rhetorical device. The bastion is the scar tissue.
hours: Always accessible from the moat and Akandia side

name: Gate of St Athanasios (Suleiman's sealed door)
sub: By tradition the Sultan rode in here on Christmas Day 1522, then had it walled up until 1922.
blurb: Built in 1441 under Grand Master de Lastic, walled shut in 1501, and by tradition the gate Suleiman rode through on Christmas Day 1522, after which he ordered it sealed again so no one could use his door; it stayed shut until 1922. The round Tower of St Mary beside it marks the west end of the English post. The moat can be entered here through a short tunnel under the inner wall. Also the way out for the walk up to Monte Smith.
dnd: The conqueror's door, sealed by the conqueror: a gate no one may use because the Sultan used it once.

name: Hafiz Ahmed Agha Library (1793)
sub: The town's arcane library: a 1540 Koran, and the 1522 siege written down by the winners.
blurb: Endowed by a village boy from Asgourou who rose to chief equerry of the sultan, 'for the literate public of his hometown'; he even paid the librarians to teach Arabic so people could read the books. About 1,260 manuscripts survive, among them a Koran of 1540 and a chronicle of the 1522 siege, with old maps of Rhodes on the walls. Courtyard and front room are free; hours are posted only on the door, and a May 2026 visitor found it locked during them because the man with the door code had gone to the hairdresser.
dnd: The spellbook vault. The only place the great siege is written down by the other side.

name: Inn of Auvergne and the Arsenal, Argyrokastrou Square
sub: The Marshal's guildhall (1507) beside the Knights' Arsenal, the Decorative Arts collection, and a heap of stone cannonballs.
blurb: Through the vaulted passage north of the Street of the Knights: the Auberge of Auvergne, completed 1507 under Guy de Blanchefort (his arms and a Gothic inscription over the door), with an outside staircase and porch. The Arsenal beside it now holds the Decorative Arts collection (08:30 to 15:30, closed Tuesdays, EUR 5); the Order's separate 14th-century first hospice also stood on this square. Behind the railings lie stone shot stockpiled for the siege. Auvergne's pilier was the Marshal, commander of the army; Grand Masters Lastic, Milly, d'Aubusson and Blanchefort all came from this small tongue.
dnd: The army's guildhall. Loot: a pile of 26-inch stone cannonballs.
hours: Exterior only; the cafe in the courtyard is reported closed

name: Malpasso, the dragon's marsh (approximate)
sub: The 'bad passage' on the coast road below Monte Smith where the legend puts the lair. Nothing to see; a trigger point.
blurb: Somewhere on the slopes and coast below Monte Smith lay Malpasso, the 'bad passage', lair of the beast that ate shepherds and knights around 1340 until Dieudonne de Gozon, forbidden by his Grand Master to try, trained two mastiffs on a wood-and-canvas dragon at his father's castle, came back and killed it. Villeneuve stripped him of the habit for disobedience, then restored it; he was Grand Master 1346 to 1353. The historian Hasluck found no source before 1521 and traced the tale to Rogation processions in which a model dragon was ritually slain; Bosio, writing in Rome in the 1590s, first attached Gozon's name. Ancient template: Diodorus says the island was once Ophiussa, the snaky one, until Apollo's oracle summoned Phorbas the Thessalian to clear it of serpents. Pin is a guess.
dnd: A quest forbidden by your own order, training on a dummy, a crocodile-skull trophy over the city gate. Schiller's moral: obedience is the Christian's ornament.

name: Tomb of the Ptolemies, Rodini (approximate)
sub: A rock-cut Hellenistic mausoleum with Doric half-columns, in a necropolis valley. Dungeon entrance, sealed sarcophagi and all.
blurb: Ten minutes up the path from Rodini Park: a 28.5 m square tomb cut into living rock with a stuccoed facade of Doric half-columns, a pedimented door, an antechamber and a burial chamber. Called 'of the Ptolemies' by tradition; really a Rhodian noble's tomb of about the 2nd century BC. Rodini itself is the Hellenistic necropolis of Korakonero, landscaped by the Italians in 1929 with dams, bridges and peacocks, and by local tradition the site of Aeschines' school of rhetoric where Cicero and Caesar studied. Coordinates approximate; 35 to 40 minutes on foot from the Old Town.
dnd: A colonnaded tomb in a valley of graves, and a wizards' college in the woods below it.

name: Our Lady of the Castle (Byzantine Museum)
sub: 11th-century Orthodox cathedral, gothicised by the Knights, then the Enderun mosque. Three consecrations on one altar.
blurb: On the north side of Museum Square: the Byzantine cathedral the Knights rebuilt in 1319 to 1334 as their Latin cathedral, later an Ottoman mosque, now the Byzantine Museum of icons and frescoes. Note the fortified apse built into the sea wall. The small Inn of England (1483, rebuilt 1919 to the old plans) stands at the square's south-east corner; the English tongue was so thin it swapped its wall-post with Aragon after 1480.
dnd: A temple of an older faith converted by the newcomers, then converted again by the conquerors.
hours: Uncertain: the Ministry page says 08:30 to 15:30, closed Tuesdays, EUR 5; the Metropolis of Rhodes says the museum is temporarily closed for reinstallation. Ask at the Palace desk.

name: Rejep Pasha Mosque, Dorieos Square
sub: The most beautiful Ottoman mosque in Rhodes (1588): Iznik tiles inside a building nobody may enter.
blurb: A single dome on a sixteen-sided drum, 16th-century Iznik tile panels inside, monolithic columns reused from Christian buildings, an octagonal fountain and the founder's tomb in the courtyard. Part of the portico collapsed in 2011 and it is closed to worship and visits. Ta Mezeklikia serves meze under the plane tree on the square beside it.
dnd: A grand vizier's crumbling tomb-mosque, tiles still glowing inside.

name: Ibrahim Pasha Mosque, Platonos Square
sub: Oldest mosque on the island (1540) and the only one still in use. Observe from the square.
blurb: Completed in 1540/41, its minaret patched by the Italians in the 1930s, formally licensed for worship only in 2019. A living place of prayer for the island's small Muslim community, so be discreet. Taverna Kostas, the locals' lunch, is two lanes away on Pythagora.
dnd: The one shrine of the old garrison still lit.

name: Yeni Hammam and Mustafa Pasha Mosque, Arionos Square
sub: The only Ottoman bath still standing in Rhodes (1558), shut for restoration. Star-pierced domes from the square.
blurb: First mentioned in a 1558 imperial decree, the women's wing added under Mustafa III, a 13 m men's dome among the largest Ottoman domes on the island. Closed for restoration for years (works were due by 31 December 2025; reopening unverified). The mosque beside it lost its minaret in 1973 and has served as the Muslim community's wedding office since 1977. Macao, the town's famous cocktail bar on this square, opens at 22:00, four hours after you sail.
dnd: A sealed bath-house of domes and steam: the locked side-dungeon under the square.

name: Governor's Palace (Palazzo del Governo)
sub: Di Fausto's 1926 Doge's Palace in white and red Lindos stone. Walk the arcade.
blurb: Centrepiece of the Foro Italico: Venetian Gothic in striped stone with Murano chandeliers inside, built to look as if it had always belonged beside the Knights' city. Seat of the Italian governors, then the Greek prefecture until 2011. The Teatro Puccini (1937) and the Casa del Fascio, now the Town Hall (1939), stand around the square. Exterior and arcade only.
dnd: The viceroy's palace of an occupying empire, deliberately built to look like it belonged to the Knights: propaganda in stone.

name: Murad Reis mosque, Ottoman cemetery and Villa Cleobolus
sub: A corsair-admiral's shrine in a graveyard of exiled khans; Lawrence Durrell's cottage in the corner.
blurb: Behind a blue door opposite the sea, next to the casino: the mosque of about 1623 and a cemetery of eucalyptus and turbaned marble stones, pilgrims once arriving with lamps and offerings; in the centre the domed tomb of Canbek Giray, Khan of Crimea, who died in exile here in 1636. In one corner is the gatekeeper's lodge Lawrence Durrell rented in 1945 and named Villa Cleobolus, where he wrote Reflections on a Marine Venus. In 1480 the Ottoman bombards fired at Fort St Nicholas from this ground. Recent visitors found the gates locked; look through the railings if so.
dnd: A haunted garden of exiles, and the bard's cottage inside the graveyard walls.

name: Aquarium of Rhodes (Hydrobiological Station)
sub: Bernabiti's 1934 Art Deco marine institute. The basement is built as an underwater cave.
blurb: At the island's northern tip: the Reale Istituto di Ricerche Biologiche, opened 1937. The tanks line a basement corridor made to feel like an underwater grotto, with black-and-white pebble floors and a 2,000-year-old monk-seal skeleton found in the port. A 30-minute stop between Elli beach and the Grande Albergo.
dnd: A sea-wizard's grotto beneath a Deco tower; the ancient seal skeleton as a bound sea-spirit.
price: EUR 7 adult from June 2026 (official fee sheet)

name: Ancient stadium and odeon, Monte Smith
sub: A 210-metre track along the meridian, where Hipparchus measured the sky and games were run for Helios.
blurb: Below the temple: the Hellenistic stadium with its curved end, officials' seats and the athletes' starting mechanism, and beside it the small marble odeon. The track runs north to south, along the meridian, which is the line Hipparchus of Nicaea worked on here between 147 and 127 BC: he saw a new star appear, dared to catalogue about 850 stars so posterity could tell if any moved, and by comparing Spica with a century-old record discovered that the whole sky wobbles, the precession of the equinoxes. The odeon is the place for the rhetoric school where Cicero declaimed in Greek and Caesar arrived late after forty days with the pirates. Walk the track for scale: the Colossus was about one-sixth of its length, lying down.
dnd: A diviner's observatory and a bards' college whose alumni include the two most dangerous men in Rome.

name: Mills Gate (often called St Catherine's Gate)
sub: Quiet harbour gate near the ship, by the ruins of St Catherine's church and the Knights' hospice.
blurb: The small harbour gate that joined the merchants' town to the grain mills on the mole, beside the ruins of St Catherine's church and the hospice built by the Italian knight Domenico d'Alemagna, rebuilt 1516 after the siege and earthquake. Old sources apply the name St Catherine's to the Marine Gate instead, so expect both names. The nearest gate to the quay if you enter this way instead of the Gate of the Virgin.

name: Romios, Sofokleous 15
sub: The fanciest kitchen open at lunch: modern Rhodian, plated. Lamb kapamas, cuttlefish risotto, octopus with orange.
blurb: Chef-owner Silouani Vlachou, born on Rhodes, revives forgotten island recipes and plates them 'as art pieces' in a lantern-lit garden. Lamb kapamas, cuttlefish risotto, chicken koulouria, octopus with orange. The pick if the birthday brief is 'modern and celebratory' rather than 'taverna'. Online booking on the restaurant's site.

name: Ta Kardasia, Platonos 4
sub: The rooftop taverna south of Hippocrates Square. Hours conflict: call before counting on a 13:00 opening.
blurb: A stone house with a small terrace above the lanes; kleftiko, vegetarian moussaka, stifado, Symi shrimp, and reviewers mention a complimentary dessert. Consistently described as 'off the tourist traps'. Sources disagree on opening time (13:00 versus 17:00); phone +30 22410 27074 the day before.
hours: 13:00 to 22:00 or 17:00 to 22:30 depending on source

name: Taverna Kostas, Pythagora 62
sub: Where locals ate inside the walls. Flagged 'temporarily closed' in September 2026: call before relying on it.
blurb: Family-run near the Ibrahim Pasha mosque with thousands of reviews and a 4.7 average: stuffed squid, moussaka, mixed dips, mains EUR 12 to 18. Both Tripadvisor and Google carried a 'temporarily closed' flag on 2 September 2026 even though reviews ran to late August. Phone +30 694 474 1226 before counting on it.
dnd: The commoners' inn of the Burgh, where the innkeeper knows every rumour.

name: Ta Mezeklikia, Dorieos Square
sub: Meze under a big shade tree beside the Rejep Pasha mosque. Cheap and cheerful.
blurb: One of the prettiest small squares in the lower town, with the tiled mosque as backdrop. Moussaka, pastitsio, souvlaki, dips; EUR 5 to 25 a head. Good for a light plate if lunch was late or big.

name: Sokratous street deli lane (melekouni, honey, souma)
sub: The bazaar street. Buy the birthday relic here: PGI melekouni, the honey-and-sesame bar of Rhodian weddings.
blurb: The old Ottoman bazaar climbing to the Suleymaniye. Small delis sell melekouni (at least 40 percent honey and 40 percent unhulled sesame, diamond-shaped, soft; the label must say PGI), thyme honey, olive oil and souma, the island's grape-pomace spirit, whose new batch is distilled in Embonas and Siana the very week of your visit. The wedding wish that comes with melekouni converts straight to a birthday: may you live as many years as there are sesame seeds in the piece. Pitaroudia, the chickpea fritters that are the island's national dish, are a lunch order, not a shop item; ask wherever you eat.
dnd: Merchant row. The genuine relic bears the PGI sigil.
price: Melekouni a few euros a bar

name: Fournariko wood-oven bakery, Sokratous 41
sub: Open all day below the clock tower. Spanakopita, orange cake, bread from Eleousa flour.
blurb: A wood oven that never goes out, on the corner of Platonos and Dinokratous: yeast-free bread, pies and portokalopita with flour from the village of Eleousa. The 'common item' of the edible quest: Rhodian bread.
dnd: The ever-burning hearth, tended in shifts.
hours: All day (the operator says 24 hours; a June 2026 field survey recorded shorter hours)

name: Koukos, Mandilara 20
sub: A 1930s house crammed with curios beside the National Theatre. Wood-oven pies and a cellar of local wine.
blurb: A rambling Rhodian guesthouse-cafe on the pedestrian street next to the 1937 Teatro Puccini, decorated floor to ceiling with old objects; the pies come out of a wood oven each morning and little cakes arrive free with your coffee. Also a cellar of Rhodian wines. The place to sit with a Greek coffee while the audio talks about the Italians.
dnd: The inn of a hundred curios, every wall a trophy shelf.
price: About EUR 19 a head for a meal

name: Wednesday farmers' market, Agios Dimitrios
sub: The producers' market runs Wednesdays and Saturdays, about 08:00 to 14:00. Honey, capers, vine leaves, cheese.
blurb: With the Nea Agora closed for restoration, this is the live market on the day: island growers on Klavdiou Pepper street by the Taxiarches cemetery and Zefyros beach, 1.5 km south of the walls. Fruit, greens, eggs, honey, home-pickled capers. Cash. Only worth it if you want to trade with villagers from the interior.
dnd: The farmers' caravan camp outside the walls.

name: Monk Coffee / The Pure Roasters, Ethnarchou Makariou 14
sub: The island's one true third-wave roastery, a few minutes uphill from the Mandraki windmills.
blurb: Single-origin espresso and filter, beans from Samba Coffee in Athens, three origins on offer, bags for sale. Order a freddo cappuccino (oat milk is good here), a flat white or an Ethiopian filter; a cappuccino is about EUR 3. Sister cafe Ara:zo does brunch. The research could not find any 'Bible Coffee' in Rhodes; this is the specialty address.
dnd: The alchemist's shop: roasted beans in glass jars, the roasters' guild sigil on the door.
hours: Mon to Sat from 08:00 (closing 19:00 or 21:00 by source); closed Sunday

name: Unik Specialty Coffee Brewers, Amerikis 42
sub: Two brothers, a tiny bar, a cold brew called the cleanest on the island, homemade halva.
blurb: Two blocks from Monk in the New Town: espresso with rich crema, a much-praised cold brew, homemade halva. Small room; go mid-morning or take it to the beach.
hours: Mon to Sat 07:30 to 19:30; closed Sunday

name: Old Town Corner Bakery, Omirou 88
sub: Croissants, baklava, orange cake, and coffee reviewers call the best inside the walls. Quiet before 10:00.
blurb: A busy corner bakery in the south-west of the walled town: croissants, baklava, portokalopita and good coffee. Handy on the way to or from the Gate of St Athanasios and the walk up to Monte Smith.

name: Porca Vacca, Agiou Fanouriou
sub: The Old Town's little cafe-gelateria. A birthday scoop on the walk back; closes 16:00.
blurb: Espresso, cappuccino and artisanal gelato on the lane of St Fanourios, saint of lost things, a few doors from the Marco Polo Mansion. Small, well loved, closes mid-afternoon.

name: Hamam Cafe, Aischylou 26
sub: A 5.0-rated garden cafe at the quiet end of Sofokleous. Honey-fried feta, tapas, strong vegan menu.
blurb: Family-run, away from the crowds, with a shady garden: honey-fried feta, dakos, salmon club sandwich, strawberry milkshakes. Ideal for a light birthday lunch or the after-lunch coffee. Despite the name it is not inside the 1558 Great Hammam, which is on Arionos Square and closed.
dnd: A courtyard of shade trees where the town's rumours are traded over coffee.

name: Yachting Club Cafe, Mandraki quay
sub: The seat, not the roast: illy coffee with the windmills, fort and deer columns in front of you.
blurb: All-day cafe on the marina edge with the classic view down the harbour, the exact vista the harbour-straddling legend was painted onto. Practical first stop between the walls and the New Town.

name: 10GR Wine Bar, Polidorou 16
sub: More than 250 Greek labels in a stone medieval house, with a Rhodian tasting flight. Opens 13:00.
blurb: Orange, sparkling, old vintages and a dedicated Rhodian flight with cheese and charcuterie. What is in the glass: PDO Rhodes whites are at least 70 percent Athiri, reds at least 70 percent Amorgiano (the local name for Mandilaria); CAIR, founded by Italians in 1928, is Greece's leading bottle-fermented sparkling producer. Street-level geocode; check the door on arrival.

name: The Wine Bar at The Wine Hotel, Platonos 41
sub: The best wine list in the walled town: CAIR and Emery labels plus small Attavyros growers.
blurb: Boutique-hotel wine bar pouring Ilios (Athiri), Grand Maitre and Chevalier de Rhodes alongside small producers from the Attavyros slopes. Ask for a glass of Athiri and one of Amorgiano. Themed flights with an oenologist by booking (+30 22410 77031).

name: Socratous Garden, Sokratous 124
sub: A walled garden with a waterfall, banana and lemon trees, behind a door off the bazaar. Drinks only.
blurb: Deep shade and fountains a step off the busiest street in town. Have a frappe or a cold beer here; recent reviews say do not eat (the moussaka arrives 'warmed up from the fridge').
dnd: A druid's grove hidden behind a bazaar door.

name: Ronda and Elli World, Elli beach lido
sub: Cocktails on the sand in Bernabiti's 1936 bathing complex, with Turkey across the strait. One drink and a swim, not a meal.
blurb: The white 1936 to 1938 Art Deco lido at the top of Elli beach, protected since 1987, now houses Ronda (07:30 to 00:00) and Elli World (08:00 to 01:00): loungers, frozen coffees, Hugo and Margarita cocktails, the diving platform offshore. Summer 2026 reviews are savage about prices and service, so treat it as one drink and the swim.

name: Vintage Wine Store, Alexandrou Diakou
sub: Where to buy the birthday bottle: a CAIR Brut or an Emery Athiri, and a bottle of souma.
blurb: Rhodian and Greek wines, spirits and souma with staff who advise, ten minutes west of Mandraki in the New Town. Souma runs around 50 percent alcohol, turns milky with water, and smells of grape rather than anise; the distillers discard both the head and the tail of each run. Anesis, a working hammam and massage centre with strong 2026 reviews, is on the same street at numbers 65 to 67 if the birthday wants steam.
dnd: The potion vendor. Souma: the mountain-still draught that halves your Wisdom save.

name: Minos Roof Garden, Omirou 5
sub: The highest terrace in the walled town, opposite a windmill. Everybody is welcome.
blurb: The roof of the Minos Pension at the top of Omirou: coffee, ice cream sundaes, beer and simple plates with the whole Old Town, the walls, the harbour and the minaret in one sweep. Better for a drink and the view than for lunch.
dnd: The watchtower tavern: from the parapet you can count every dome and bastion of the fortress-town.

name: Castello House rooftop, Orfeos 50
sub: Rooftop since 1975 under the Suleymaniye minaret and the clock tower. A view lunch or a drink.
blurb: At the top of the bazaar beside the mosque: kleftiko, moussaka, swordfish on a roof terrace with minaret and clock tower views. Open in season from 10:00; service can lag at peak. Use it for the visual, not the main meal.

name: La Veranda, Square of the Jewish Martyrs
sub: Family-run rooftop over the memorial square, closest to the ship. Open from 10:00.
blurb: Several flights of stairs to terraces above the square with the Palace on the skyline and the sea in the distance. Octopus, calamari, seafood spaghetti; consistent rather than gastronomic, and useful because it absorbs any timing.

name: Monte Smith ridge viewpoint
sub: The whole west coast and the Turkish mountains. The lookout hill of every empire since the founding.
blurb: The ridge above the acropolis, named for the admiral who watched here for Napoleon's fleet. Kebric's point is that only from this hill can you watch a full day's arc of the sun over the sea, which is why the city of Helios put its sacred heart up here. Late-afternoon light is the best you will get, since sunset is after sailing.

name: Elli beach and the diving platform
sub: The town beach at the island's tip. A late-September swim, and Durrell's beach.
blurb: Spearhead-shaped pebble beach from the casino to the Aquarium, with a swim-out diving platform anchored offshore. The sea is warmest in September. Sunbeds and bars in season, softer prices at the end of it. 25 minutes from Hippocrates Square along the Mandraki promenade.

name: Moat entrance at Mandraki (St Paul's Gate gardens)
sub: Northern entry to the dry moat: about 2.5 km of lawns, cannonballs and bastions to the Akandia Gate. Free, always open.
blurb: The Knights' dry moat, never filled with water, about 30 m wide under walls up to 12 m thick, now a landscaped park with sandy paths, an open-air theatre and stone shot lying where it fell. Walk clockwise under the d'Amboise Gate, past the St George bastion, the Tower of Spain and the English curtain to the del Carretto bastion and the Akandia Gate beside the port: 60 to 90 minutes, and the view an attacking army had. Stairways also drop in at the gates of St Anthony and St Athanasios.
dnd: The killing ground. After hearing about the walls from inside, descend into what the besiegers had to cross.

name: Akandia Gate: southern moat entrance
sub: The Italians cut this gate through the Italian terreplein in 1935. Five minutes from the quay.
blurb: The southern way into the moat, beside the del Carretto bastion and close to the cruise quays. If the ship berths at Akandia, this is the nearest gate, and the moat walk can be done first thing in the cool of the morning, ending at Mandraki.

name: Rodini Park
sub: A shaded ravine 3 km south: Hellenistic necropolis, Italian dams and bridges of 1929, peacocks. Skip if the day is tight.
blurb: The necropolis of Korakonero re-landscaped by the Italians with lakes and bridges, locally billed as the world's first landscaped park, and by tradition the site of Aeschines' school of rhetoric. Free; reviews describe neglect. The rock-cut Tomb of the Ptolemies is ten minutes up the path. Bus 3 from the market, or 35 to 40 minutes on foot.

name: Kallithea Springs (Thermes Kallitheas)
sub: Italian Art Deco spa of 1929 on a rocky cove. Swim off the mosaics; a taxi 15 minutes south. EUR 5.
blurb: Pietro Lombardi's 1929 Regie Terme with Armando Bernabiti's decoration: a small rotunda with six Moorish gates and a statue of Eros, a great rotunda with an elliptical arcade over the bay, every path a black-and-white pebble mosaic. A German prison camp in the war, a ruin by 1967 (The Guns of Navarone was shot here), restored 1999 to 2007. The springs have dried; it is a swimming cove now, with a cafe-bar and sunbeds at the water. Rocky entry, so swim shoes. Taxi about EUR 15 to 20 each way; bus EUR 2.50.
dnd: An abandoned temple of a healing god at the water's edge: mosaic wards underfoot, a dry sacred spring, a shrine to Eros, and a wartime prison layer for the haunted second act.
price: EUR 5; sunbed pair about EUR 25 to 30

name: Grande Albergo delle Rose (Casino Rodos)
sub: Lago's 1927 'Dream of the East'. Where Ralph Bunche brokered the Egypt-Israel armistice in 1949. A martini in the lobby bar.
blurb: Di Fausto's grand hotel, opened 24 May 1927 in Byzantine, Arab, Ottoman and Venetian lines, stripped of its ornament by the next governor in 1936, reborn as Casino Rodos. From January to February 1949 the UN mediator Ralph Bunche negotiated the Israel-Egypt armistice here (the Jordanian one was formally signed here too); he had a local potter make plates for each negotiator and told Moshe Dayan he would have broken them over their heads. Nobel Peace Prize, 1950. For a non-gambler: the ground-floor lounge bar, the beach restaurant on the north sand, or the pan-Asian restaurant in the garden. The casino: 21 and over, passport registration, entry reported free in 2025 to 2026, no swimwear or hats.
dnd: A gilded neutral-ground inn where rival kingdoms signed a truce under a foreign mediator; the casino floor as a den of chance-gods.
hours: Hotel year-round; bar hours not published (call +30 22410 57700)

name: Stani, Agias Anastasias 28
sub: The town's beloved dairy-patisserie. Mastic and wild-cherry ice cream, milk pie, baklava. Brisk service, superb product.
blurb: Rhodes' classic zacharoplasteio just south of the walls, famous for ice cream (stracciatella, or mastic with wild cherry) and the milk pie. The founding legends online could not be verified, so enjoy the ice cream rather than the history. About 700 m south of the Gate of St John.

name: Mandraki boat quay: private sailing
sub: A skippered sailing boat for two hours from about EUR 260, or a 4-hour east-coast cruise at 09:45 for EUR 60.
blurb: Excursion boats line the inner Mandraki quay below the Nea Agora. Rhodes Rent a Boat (+30 695 166 6454) runs a semi-private east-coast cruise with swim stops at Kallithea and Anthony Quinn Bay, departing 09:45 and back around 13:45, or private skippered sailing from EUR 260 for two hours, up to ten guests. A birthday-sized splurge that trades the Old Town morning for the water. Book ahead.
price: EUR 60 per person semi-private; private from EUR 260

name: Akandia cruise quay (alternate berth)
sub: If the ship's app says Akandia, you land here: ten minutes further from the gates. Nearest gate is Akandia Gate.
blurb: The newer cruise quays on the Akandia mole south-east of the walls. From here walk north-west along the waterfront; the Akandia Gate and the moat are about six minutes, the Gate of the Virgin about ten. The route on this map assumes the Tourist Port; only the first leg changes.

name: Rimini Square taxi rank
sub: Taxis for Kallithea (about EUR 15 to 20) or Monte Smith (about 10 minutes). Agree the fare first.
blurb: The main rank by the Nea Agora, plus taxis at the cruise terminal. Metered tariff: EUR 3.72 flag including the first 2.7 km, then EUR 0.90 per km by day, with a small port surcharge; drivers quote fixed prices for the standard runs. Hop-on hop-off buses also leave from here.

name: Nea Agora (New Market): closed for restoration
sub: Di Fausto's seven-sided market of 1926 shut on 17 November 2025 for a full rebuild. Look, do not plan to eat.
blurb: The Italian market-fortress with its domed fish-market pavilion in the courtyard: shops shut in November 2025, works from January 2026, 52 interior shops demolished and services re-laid; still a building site in August 2026, with the first merchants expected back in October for fit-out and the first openings gambled on Christmas. On 30 September expect restored facades and a locked or half-open courtyard. View the great Gothic gate from the Mandraki side.
dnd: The bazaar-fortress is sealed and being re-warded by masons.

name: Hatzikelis (caution on fish pricing)
sub: The first restaurant inside the port gate, in an 1853 Jewish-built house. Fresh fish, but 2026 complaints of 'different menus'.
blurb: The 1982 fish taverna beside the Juderia that the earlier plan pencilled in for lunch. Fresh fish, shrimp in ouzo cream, seafood risotto and shade, but a May 2026 review reported being shown a different menu with higher prices, and an August 2025 family of four paid EUR 216 and judged it not worth it. If you go, ask for the printed price list before ordering fish by weight. Nireas and Romios are five minutes away.
price: Fish by weight can run high

name: Marco Polo Mansion (dinner only)
sub: The most romantic room in Rhodes opens at 19:00, an hour after you sail. Walk past and tell the story.
blurb: An Ottoman-era Turkish house with its harem and original wardrobes, restored by Efi Dede and the artist Giuseppe Sala, with a candlelit courtyard of citrus and vines. Sea bass ceviche, lamb croquettes, pasta with sea urchin. Garden dinner only, 48 hours' booking. The same is true of Nomad (opens 18:30) and Tamam in the New Town (17:00); The Ritualist on Sofokleous opens at 15:00 as a late-lunch fallback.
price: About EUR 85 to 170 for two with wine

name: Paneri, Platonos Square (verify lunch hours)
sub: Creative Mediterranean cooking, 4.9 from about 1,200 reviews, ten metres from Ta Kardasia. Hours unchecked.
blurb: Surfaced by the fact-checkers as the most plausible plated, celebratory lunch inside the walls now that Dinoris has left Museum Square for a dinner-only room in the New Town. Highly rated but nobody verified a midday opening; call before building the birthday around it. Same square as Ta Kardasia.

name: Pervola open-air museum: the secret dockyards (new, June 2026)
sub: Twenty stremmata sealed for 75 years, opened June 2026: Hellenistic shipsheds, the Roman cardo and tetrapylon, a 700-piece sculpture yard.
blurb: Between the Palace and the Liberty Gate, on the seaward side of the moat, a zone used as a depot for 75 years opened to the public on 14 June 2026: the Hellenistic shipsheds of the military harbour, the Roman main street with its four-way arch, a medieval church, the Italian governor's gardens, and an outdoor gallery of some 700 carved stones. This is the ground Strabo wrote about: some of the Rhodian dockyards were kept hidden and forbidden to the people, and death was the penalty for anyone who spied on them or went inside. In 204 BC an agent of Philip of Macedon posed as a defector and, on a rough windy night, burned thirteen sheds with the ships inside. Hours and any fee were not published; the Palace gardens are listed 09:00 to 17:00, so ask at the Palace desk. If it is closed, the fenced excavation is visible from the pavement of Eleftherias street.
dnd: A stone-yard of 4,000 catalogued fragments laid over slipways where triremes were built, guarded by a law that killed spies. The sabotage adventure writes itself.
hours: Unpublished; Palace gardens 09:00 to 17:00. Ask at the Palace desk.

name: Seaside walkway on the harbour walls (new, June 2026)
sub: A restored corridor along the sea wall from the Mills Gate to St Paul's Gate: the direct route from the quay to Mandraki, and the fallback if the walls walk is shut.
blurb: Delivered on 10 June 2026: the Apostle Paul bastion, the fortifications of the Naillac mole, the Byzantine sea-gate complex, a spiral stair at the new sea gate and the upper level of the Mills Gate, with an accessible corridor along the walls and lighting. It runs from two minutes off the cruise mole to the root of the Naillac mole, about fifteen minutes, past the Marine Gate. No hours were published; it was framed as public space. Combined with the moat from the d'Amboise Gate, it is a free unticketed substitute if the rampart walk turns out to be closed.
dnd: The seaward curtain of the fortress, the way the Genoese came in by night in 1248.

name: Agios Fanourios, Dorieos Square (the saint of lost things)
sub: A 13th-century domed church, open 07:00 to 19:00, home of the island's patron. Light a candle, name what you lost, then go find cake.
blurb: A working parish in a small cross-shaped church built on Late Roman remains, with three layers of fresco: early 13th century in the sanctuary, a Last Judgement of 1335 over the tombs by the door with the donors painted in paradise, and a 15th-century layer. A mosque under the Ottomans, dedicated to Fanourios only in 1946. The saint was unknown until his icon came out of the rubble of a wall repair with its colours intact, a young soldier ringed by twelve tortures; he is the saint who reveals what was lost. Greeks bake a lenten orange-and-walnut cake, fanouropita, cut it into forty pieces and make a wish. Beside the Rejep Pasha mosque; Ta Mezeklikia is on the same square.
dnd: The relic that outlived every regime, and a quest-giver whose whole job is finding what was lost.

name: Agia Aikaterini, 'Ilk Mihrab' (Suleiman's first prayer)
sub: A 14th-century church where, by tradition, the Sultan said his first prayer in the captured city. Frescoes of a saint broken on the wheel.
blurb: Three aisles and four building phases from the 14th century on Perikleous street, between the Jewish quarter and the Red Gate. Its Ottoman name, Ilk Mihrab, the first prayer niche, records the tradition that Suleiman prayed here first in the winter of 1522. Inside, locked most of the time: Peter and Paul at the door, four healer saints painted after a plague, a kneeling donor couple offering a model of the church, and a cycle of the life of St Catherine unique in the East.
dnd: The conqueror's first prayer, in a church painted with a saint broken on the wheel.

name: Gate of the early Byzantine castle (top of Agiou Fanouriou street)
sub: Where the lane climbs into the Street of the Knights, an arch marks the door between the Byzantine inner ward and the outer town.
blurb: The Byzantine city of the 7th to 13th centuries had three parts: the citadel on the Palace hill, the fortified upper town, and an outer town that only came inside the walls in the 12th century. This arched passage is the gate in the south wall of that upper town; two early Byzantine towers survive embedded in Hospitaller houses fifty metres west. Look at the change in the masonry. Between the Fourth Crusade and the Knights, a local magnate ruled from up here as Caesar Gabalas, Lord of Rhodes and the Cyclades, whose coins called him the emperor's servant while he swore fealty to Venice.
dnd: The portal from the outer bailey into the keep district; a rogue baron's seat before the paladins arrived.

name: Filerimos: monastery and the betrayed citadel (taxi, 23 minutes)
sub: The better half-day than Lindos: EUR 24 by taxi, EUR 10 entry, open to 20:00, nobody bussed there in waves. Four civilisations in thirty paces.
blurb: The acropolis of ancient Ialysos, 14 km south-west. In the monastery courtyard the cross-shaped font of a 5th-century basilica sits on the stylobate of the temple of Athena; beside it the Knights' church, whose south chapel held the icon of Our Lady of Philermos, the talisman of medieval Rhodes, until it was lashed to the mainmast of a captured carrack in January 1523; around it the Italian Franciscan cloister of 1931. On 11 November 1306 the Knights took the citadel here through the treason of a local Greek and killed its 300 Turkish mercenaries, then besieged the city from this rock for four years. A cypress-lined Way of the Cross leads to a concrete cross with the whole west coast below; hundreds of peacocks; and at the car-park kiosk the friars' seven-herb liqueur, Sette Erbe. Lindos, by contrast, is 65 minutes each way with timed EUR 20 tickets and the coaches from both ships.
dnd: A hilltop keep of four phases, a garrison betrayed from within, a relic that escaped on a captured ship, and a potion-seller at the gate.
hours: 08:00 to 20:00 (official summer schedule); taxi about EUR 24 each way, waiting EUR 11.90 an hour

name: St George Chostos, Filerimos (the underground chapel)
sub: A crypt cut into the rock over a sealed spring, painted with kneeling knights, armoured skulls and Death prevailing over a knight.
blurb: A Byzantine crypt whose sacred spring was sealed and whose cistern became a 15th-century burial chapel for a Frankish family close to Grand Master d'Aubusson. Frescoes: Hospitallers and their families kneeling with their patron saints, St Michael killing the dragon, skulls in armour with the Order's arms, and Death prevailing over a knight. Listed as open every day; carry a phone torch. Thirty metres below the plateau's south edge, down a stone stair, a 4th-century BC fountain house with six Doric columns and lion-head spouts, buried by a landslide until 1923, with water tunnels behind it that served as a hiding place in troubled times.
dnd: A sealed spring beneath a crypt painted with armoured skulls, and a lion-mouthed fountain with tunnels behind it: the campaign's dungeon entrance.
